21. Avoid Scheduling Failures

作者：Norman Carnovale

Failed projects can happen for a multitude of reasons. One of the most common sources of failure is altering the project schedule in midstream without proper planning. This kind of failure is avoidable, but it can require major effort on the part of multiple people. Adjusting the timeline or increasing resources on a project are not normally of concern. Problems start when you are asked to do more in the same timeline or when the schedule is shortened without reducing the workload.

项目失败的原因有很多。最常见的失败原因之一是在中途未经妥善规划就改动项目进度。这种失败是可以避免的，但可能需要多人付出巨大努力。调整时间线或增加资源通常不是问题。问题出现在你被要求在同样的时间线里做更多事，或者工作量不减但进度被缩短的时候。

The idea that schedules can be shortened in order to reduce cost or speed up delivery is a very common misconception. You’ll commonly see attempts to require overtime or sacrifice “less important scheduled tasks” (like unit testing) as a way to reduce delivery dates, or increase functionality while keeping the delivery dates as is. Avoid this scenario at all costs. Remind those requesting the changes of the following facts:

以为缩短进度就能降本或加速交付，是非常常见的误解。你经常会看到有人要求加班、或牺牲「不那么重要的计划任务」（比如单元测试）来缩短交付日期，或者在保持交付日期不变的情况下增加功能。不惜一切代价避免这种场景。提醒要求改动的人以下事实：

A rushed design schedule leads to poor design, bad documentation, and • probable quality assurance or user acceptance problems.

仓促的设计进度导致设计差、文档差，以及很可能出现质量保证或用户验收问题。

A rushed coding or delivery schedule has a direct relationship to the • number of bugs delivered to the users.

仓促的编码或交付进度与交付给用户的 bug 数量直接相关。

A rushed test schedule leads to poorly tested code and has a direct rela- • tionship to the number of testing issues encountered.

仓促的测试进度导致测试不充分，与遇到的测试问题数量直接相关。

All of the above lead to production issues, which are much more expensive • to fix.

以上所有都会导致生产问题，而修复这些问题要贵得多。

The end result is an increase in cost as opposed to a reduction. This is normally why the failures happen.

最终结果是成本上升而不是下降。失败通常就是这么发生的。

As an architect you will one day find yourself in the position of having to act quickly to increase the likelihood of success. Speak up early. First try to maintain quality by negotiating the originally planned timeline. If a shortened schedule is necessary, then try to move noncritical functionality to future release(s). Obviously this will take good preparation, negotiating skills, and a knack for influencing people. Prepare by sharpening your skills in those areas today. You will be glad you did.

作为架构师，总有一天你会发现自己必须迅速行动以提高成功概率。尽早发声。先通过谈判争取维持原计划时间线来保证质量。如果必须缩短进度，那就把非关键功能挪到未来版本。显然这需要充分准备、谈判技巧和影响力。今天就开始磨练这些技能。你会庆幸自己这么做。

Norman Carnovale Norman Carnovale is an IT architect working for Lockheed Martin Professional Services on Homeland Security–related projects. He was formerly a software consultant, instructor, and architect for Davalen, LLC (http://www.davalen.com), a Premier IBM Business Partner specializing in WebSphere Portlet Factory, WebSphere Portal, and Lotus Domino projects.

Norman Carnovale Norman Carnovale 是洛克希德·马丁专业服务公司的 IT 架构师，做国土安全相关项目。他之前是 Davalen, LLC（一家专注 WebSphere Portlet Factory、WebSphere Portal 和 Lotus Domino 项目的 IBM 顶级业务合作伙伴）的软件顾问、讲师和架构师。

22. Architectural Tradeoffs

作者：Mark Richards

Every software architect should know and understand that you can’t have it all. It is virtually impossible to design an architecture that has high performance, high availability, a high level of security, and a high degree of abstraction all at the same time. There is a true story that software architects should know, understand, and be able to communicate to clients and colleagues. It is the story of a ship called the Vasa .

每个软件架构师都应该知道并理解：你不可能什么都要。想同时设计出高性能、高可用、高安全、高抽象的架构，几乎不可能。有一个真实故事软件架构师应该知道、理解、并能讲给客户和同事听。那就是瓦萨号战船的故事。

In the 1620s Sweden and Poland were at war. Wanting a quick end to this costly war, the king of Sweden commissioned the building of a ship called the Vasa . Now, this was no ordinary ship. The requirements for this ship were unlike any other ship of that time; it was to be more than 200 feet long, carry 64 guns on two gun decks, and have the ability to transport 300 troops safely across the waters into Poland. Time was of the essence, and money was tight (sound familiar?). The ship architect had never designed such a ship before. Smaller, single-gun deck ships were his area of expertise. Nevertheless, the ship’s architect extrapolated on his prior experience and set out designing and building the Vasa . The ship was eventually built to specifications, and when the eventful day came for the launch, the ship proudly sailed into the harbor, fired its gun salute, and promptly sank to the bottom of the ocean.

1620 年代瑞典和波兰在交战。瑞典国王想尽快结束这场代价高昂的战争，下令建造一艘叫瓦萨号的船。这不是一艘普通的船。这艘船的要求在当时前所未有：长 200 多英尺，两层炮甲板载 64 门炮，还要能安全运送 300 名士兵渡海进入波兰。时间紧迫，钱也紧（耳熟吗？）。造船师从没设计过这种船。他的专长是更小的单层炮甲板船。尽管如此，造船师还是根据过往经验外推，开始设计和建造瓦萨号。船最终按规格造好了，在那个重要的下水日，船骄傲地驶入港口，鸣放礼炮，然后迅速沉入海底。

The problem with the Vasa was obvious; anyone who has ever seen the deck of a large fighting ship from the 1600s and 1700s knows that the decks on those

瓦萨号的问题很明显；任何见过 16、17 世纪大型战船甲板的人都知道那些

ships were crowded and unsafe, particularly in battle. Building a ship that was both a fighting ship and a transport ship was a costly mistake. The ship’s architect, in an attempt to fulfill all of the king’s wishes, created an unbalanced and unstable ship.

甲板拥挤而危险，尤其在战斗中。把船同时建成战船和运输船是个代价高昂的错误。造船师为了满足国王所有愿望，造出了一艘不平衡、不稳定的船。

Software architects can learn a lot from this story and apply this unfortunate event to the design of software architecture. Trying to fulfill each and every requirement (as with the Vasa ) creates an unstable architecture that essentially accomplishes nothing well. A good example of a tradeoff is the requirement to make a service-oriented architecture (SOA) perform as well as a point-topoint solution. Doing so usually requires you to bypass the various levels of abstraction created by an SOA approach, thereby creating an architecture that looks something like what you would typically order at your local Italian restaurant. There are several tools available to architects to determine what the tradeoffs should be when designing an architecture. Two popular methods are the Architecture Tradeoff Analysis Method (ATAM) and the Cost Benefit Analysis Method (CBAM). You can learn more about ATAM and CBAM by visiting the Software Engineering Institute (SEI) websites at http://www.sei. cmu.edu/architecture/ata_method.html and http://www.sei.cmu.edu/architecture/cbam.html , respectively.

软件架构师可以从这个故事中学到很多，把这个不幸事件应用到软件架构设计中。试图满足每一个需求（像瓦萨号那样）会造出一个什么都做不好的不稳定架构。权衡的一个好例子是：要求面向服务架构（SOA）达到点对点方案的性能。这么做通常需要你绕过 SOA 引入的各层抽象，结果架构看起来就像你在本地意大利餐厅会点的那种东西（注：指层层叠叠的意面）。架构师有几种工具来决定设计架构时该做什么权衡。两种流行方法是架构权衡分析方法（ATAM）和成本收益分析方法（CBAM）。你可以访问软件工程研究所（SEI）网站了解更多。

23. Database As a Fortress

作者：Dan Chak

The database is where all of the data, both input by your employees and collected from your customers, resides. User interfaces, business and application logic, and even employees will come and go, but your data lasts forever. Consequently, enough cannot be said about the importance of building a solid data model from Day One.

数据库是你员工输入、从客户收集的所有数据的所在地。用户界面、业务和应用逻辑、甚至员工都会来来去去，但你的数据永存。因此，从第一天起就建立稳固数据模型的重要性，再怎么强调都不为过。

The exuberance over agile techniques has left many thinking that it’s fine, or even preferable, to design applications as you go. Gone are the days of writing complex, comprehensive technical designs up front! The new school says deploy early and often. A line of code in production is better than 10 in your head. It seems almost too good to be true, and where your data is concerned, it is.

对敏捷技术的狂热让很多人觉得边走边设计应用也没什么、甚至更好。提前写复杂全面技术设计的日子一去不复返了！新学派说早部署、勤部署。生产环境里一行代码胜过你脑子里十行。这好得近乎不真实，而在数据这件事上，它确实不真实。

While business rules and user interfaces do evolve rapidly, the structures and relationships within the data you collect often do not. Therefore, it is critical to have your data model defined right from the start, both structurally and analytically. Migrating data from one schema to another in situ is difficult at best, time consuming always, and error prone often. While you can suffer bugs temporarily at the application layer, bugs in the database can be disastrous. Finding and fixing a data-layer design problem does not restore your data once it has been corrupted.

虽然业务规则和用户界面确实快速演化，但你收集的数据内部的结构和关系往往不演化。因此，从一开始就把数据模型在结构和分析上都定义对，至关重要。把数据从一个 schema 原地迁移到另一个，最好情况下也很困难，总是耗时，还经常出错。应用层的 bug 你可以临时忍受，数据库的 bug 却可能是灾难性的。一旦数据被破坏，找到并修复数据层设计问题也恢复不了你的数据。

A solid data model is one that guarantees security of today’s data, but is also extensible for tomorrow’s. Guaranteeing security means being impervious to bugs that will—despite your best efforts—be pervasive in an ever-changing application layer. It means enforcing referential integrity. It means building in domain constraints wherever they are known. It means choosing appropriate

稳固的数据模型既要保证今天数据的安全，也要为明天可扩展。保证安全意味着对那些——尽管你尽全力——在不断变化的应用层里必然存在的 bug 免疫。它意味着强制引用完整性。它意味着在任何已知的地方内建领域约束。它意味着选择合适的

keys that help you ensure your data’s referential integrity and constraint satisfaction. Being extensible for tomorrow means properly normalizing your data so that you can easily add architectural layers upon your data model later. It means not taking shortcuts.

键来帮助你确保数据的引用完整性和约束满足。为明天可扩展意味着正确规范化数据，以便之后能在数据模型上轻松加架构层。它意味着不抄近路。

The database is the final gatekeeper of your precious data. The application layer, which is by design ephemeral, cannot be its own watchdog. For the database to keep proper guard, the data model must be designed to reject data that does not belong, and to prevent relationships that do not make sense. Keys, foreign key relationships, and domain constraints, when described in a schema, are succinct, easy to understand and verify, and ultimately selfdocumenting. Domain rules encoded in the data model are also physical and persistent; a change to application logic does not wash them away.

数据库是你宝贵数据的最终守门人。应用层本质上是短暂的，不能自己当自己的看门狗。数据库要尽职守卫，数据模型就必须设计成拒绝不属于的数据、阻止不合理的关系。键、外键关系和领域约束，一旦写进 schema，就是简洁、易理解、易验证、最终自文档化的。编码进数据模型的领域规则也是物理的、持久的；应用逻辑的改变冲不走它们。

To get the most out of a relational database—to make it a true part of the application as opposed to simply a storehouse for application data—you need to have a solid understanding of what you are building from the start. As your product evolves, so too will the data layer, but at each phase of its evolution, it should always maintain its status as Fortress. If you trust it and bestow upon it the heavy responsibility of trapping bugs from other layers of your application, you will never be disappointed.

要充分发挥关系数据库的威力——让它成为应用真正的一部分，而不只是应用数据的仓库——你从一开始就需要对自己在构建什么有扎实理解。随着产品演化，数据层也会演化，但在演化的每个阶段，它都应该保持堡垒的地位。如果你信任它、把拦截应用其他层 bug 的重任交给它，你永远不会失望。

Dan Chak Dan Chak is the director of software development at CourseAdvisor Inc., a Washington Post company. He is the author of Enterprise Rails (O’Reilly).

Dan Chak Dan Chak 是 CourseAdvisor Inc.（华盛顿邮报旗下公司）的软件开发总监。他著有《Enterprise Rails》（O'Reilly）。

24. Use Uncertainty As a Driver

作者：Kevlin Henney

Confronted with two options, most people think that the most important thing to do is to make a choice between them. In design (software or otherwise), it is not. The presence of two options is an indicator that you need to consider uncertainty in the design. Use the uncertainty as a driver to determine where you can defer commitment to details and where you can partition and abstract to reduce the significance of design decisions. If you hardwire the first thing that comes to mind, you’re more likely to be stuck with it, so that incidental decisions become significant and the softness of the software is reduced.

面对两个选项，大多数人认为最重要的是在两者间做选择。在设计中（软件或其他），不是这样。两个选项的存在，标志着你需要在设计中考虑不确定性。用不确定性作为驱动力，决定哪里可以推迟对细节的承诺、哪里可以拆分和抽象以降低设计决策的重要性。如果你把第一个冒出来的想法硬编码进去，你更可能被它困住，于是偶然决策变得重要，软件的柔性降低。

One of the simplest and most constructive definitions of architecture comes from Grady Booch: “All architecture is design but not all design is architecture. Architecture represents the significant design decisions that shape a system, where significant is measured by cost of change.” What follows from this is that an effective architecture is one that generally reduces the significance of design decisions. An ineffective architecture will amplify significance.

关于架构最简单也最有建设性的定义之一来自 Grady Booch：「所有架构都是设计，但不是所有设计都是架构。架构代表塑造一个系统的重要设计决策，而重要性以变更成本衡量。」由此推论，有效的架构是那种普遍降低设计决策重要性的架构。无效的架构会放大重要性。

When a design decision can reasonably go one of two ways, an architect needs to take a step back. Instead of trying to decide between options A and B, the question becomes “How do I design so that the choice between A and B is less significant?” The most interesting thing is not actually the choice between A and B, but the fact that there is a choice between A and B (and that the appropriate choice is not necessarily obvious or stable).

当一个设计决策合理地可能走两条路之一时，架构师需要退一步。与其试图在 A 和 B 之间做选择，问题变成「我怎么设计才能让 A 和 B 之间的选择变得不那么重要？」最有意思的其实不是 A 和 B 之间的选择，而是「存在 A 和 B 之间的选择」这个事实（而且合适的选择未必显然或稳定）。

An architect may need to go in circles before becoming dizzy and recognizing the dichotomy. Standing at a whiteboard (energetically) debating options with a colleague? Umming and ahhing in front of some code, deadlocked over whether to try one implementation or another? When a new requirement or a clarification of a requirement has cast doubt on the wisdom of a current implementation, that’s uncertainty. Respond by figuring out what separation or encapsulation would isolate that decision from the code that ultimately depends on it. Without this sensibility the alternative response is often rambling code that, like a nervous interviewee, babbles away trying to compensate for uncertainty with a multitude of speculative and general options. Or, where a response is made with arbitrary but unjustified confidence, a wrong turn is taken at speed and without looking back.

架构师可能需要绕几圈才会头晕、认出这个二分法。在白板前（精力充沛地）和同事争论选项？在代码前嗯嗯啊啊，在尝试这个实现还是那个实现上僵持？当一个新需求或对需求的澄清让当前实现的智慧受到质疑，那就是不确定性。应对方法是：找出什么样的分离或封装能把这个决策和最终依赖它的代码隔离开。没有这种感觉，另一种常见反应是写出漫无边际的代码——像紧张的面试者，用一堆投机性、泛化的选项来弥补不确定性。或者，当一个人带着武断但毫无根据的自信做决定时，他就会高速、头也不回地走错路。

There is often pressure to make a decision for the decision’s sake. This is where options thinking can help. Where there is uncertainty over different paths a system’s development might take, make the decision not to make a decision. Defer the actual decision until a decision can be made more responsibly, based on actual knowledge, but not so late that it is not possible to take advantage of that knowledge.

经常有压力要为做决定而做决定。这时候选项思维能帮上忙。当系统开发可能走向不同路径而存在不确定性时，做「不做决定」的决定。把实际决定推迟到能基于真实知识更负责任地做决定的时候，但也不要晚到无法利用那个知识。

Architecture and process are interwoven, which is a key reason that architects should favor development lifecycles and architectural approaches that are empirical and elicit feedback, using uncertainty constructively to divide up both the system and the schedule.

架构和过程是交织在一起的，这就是为什么架构师应该偏好经验性、能引出反馈的开发生命周期和架构方法，建设性地利用不确定性来划分系统和进度。

25. Warning: Problems in Mirror May Be Larger Than They Appear

作者：Dave Quick

I’ve worked on hundreds of software projects. Every one had issues that caused more problems than the team expected. Often, a small part of the team identified the issue early on and the majority dismissed or ignored it because they didn’t understand how important it really was until it was too late.

我做过几百个软件项目。每个项目都出过问题，而且问题比团队预期的多。经常是团队里一小部分人很早就发现了问题，但大多数人因为没意识到它有多重要而 dismiss 或忽略了，等到太晚。

The forces at work include:

起作用的力量包括：

Issues that seemed trivial early in the project become critical after it is too • late to fix them. While the boiling frog experiment may be folklore, it’s a useful analogy for what happens in many projects.

项目早期看似微不足道的问题，等到修复太晚时变成关键问题。煮青蛙的实验也许是传说，但对很多项目里发生的事是个有用的类比。

Individuals often face resistance when the rest of the team does not share • their experience or knowledge. Overcoming this resistance requires unusual courage, confidence, and persuasiveness. It rarely happens, even with highly paid, experienced consultants specifically hired to help avoid such problems.

当团队其他人不共享他们的经验或知识时，个人经常遇到阻力。克服这种阻力需要非凡的勇气、自信和说服力。这很少发生，即使是高薪请来专门帮避免这类问题的经验丰富的顾问。

Most software developers are optimists. Painful experience teaches us to • temper our optimism, but without specific experience we tend toward optimism. Natural pessimists on development teams are often unpopular, even if they are consistently right. Few people will risk this reputation and take a stand against the majority without a very solid case. Most of us have had the “This makes me uncomfortable, but I can’t explain why” feeling, but sharing it rarely wins any arguments.

大多数软件开发是乐观主义者。痛苦的经验教会我们调和乐观，但没有具体经验时我们倾向乐观。开发团队里天生悲观的人往往不受欢迎，即使他们一直是对的。很少有人会冒着这种声誉、在没有非常确凿证据的情况下站出来反对多数。我们大多数人都有过「这让我不舒服，但我说不清为什么」的感觉，但说出来很少能赢得争论。

Every team member has a different view of what is more or less important. • Their concerns are often focused on their personal responsibilities, not the project’s goals.

每个团队成员对什么更重要、什么不那么重要有不同看法。他们关注的通常是自己的个人职责，而不是项目目标。

We all have blind spots, shortcomings that are difficult for us to recognize • or to accept.

我们都有盲点——那些我们自己很难识别或接受的缺点。

Some possible strategies to counteract these forces could include:

对抗这些力量的一些可能策略包括：

Establish an organized approach to • managing risks. One simple approach is to track risks the same way you track bugs. Anyone can identify a risk, and each risk is tracked until it is no longer a risk. Risks are prioritized and reviewed when their status changes or when there is new information. This helps remove emotion from the discussion and makes it easier to remember to re-evaluate risks periodically.

建立有组织的风险管理方法。一个简单方法是像跟踪 bug 一样跟踪风险。任何人都能识别风险，每个风险一直跟踪到它不再是风险。风险被排优先级，状态变化或有新信息时评审。这有助于把情绪从讨论中去掉，也更容易记得定期重新评估风险。

When going against the majority, look for ways to help the rest of the team • understand more easily. Encourage any team you’re on to recognize the value in dissenting opinions and look for neutral ways to discuss them.

当你反对多数时，想办法帮团队其他人更容易理解。鼓励你所在的任何团队认识到异议的价值，并找中立的方式讨论。

“Bad smells” are worth recognizing. If the facts aren’t there yet, look for • the simplest tests that would provide the facts.

「坏味道」值得识别。如果事实还没有，找能提供事实的最简单测试。

Constantly test your understanding against the team and the customer. • Tools such as a prioritized list of user stories can help, but are no substitute for regular communications with the customer and an open mind.

不断用团队和客户检验你的理解。像排了优先级的用户故事列表这样的工具有帮助，但不能替代和客户定期沟通和开放心态。

Blind spots are, by definition, hard to recognize. People you trust to tell • you the hard truth when you need it are a precious resource.

盲点，顾名思义，很难识别。在你需要时能告诉你硬话的人，是宝贵资源。

Dave Quick Dave Quick is the owner, chief architect, janitor, and sole employee of Thoughtful Arts. Thoughtful Arts develops off-the-shelf software for musicians and provides software design consulting for companies who develop music, or arts-oriented software.

Dave Quick Dave Quick 是 Thoughtful Arts 的所有者、首席架构师、勤杂工和唯一员工。Thoughtful Arts 为音乐家开发现成软件，并为开发音乐或艺术导向软件的公司提供软件设计咨询。

26. Reuse Is About People and Education, Not Just Architecture

作者：Jeremy Meyer

You might adopt the approach  that a framework that is well designed, or an architecture that is carefully considered and cleverly implemented, will lend itself to reuse within your organization. The truth is that even the most beautiful, elegant, and reusable architecture, framework, or system will only be reused by people who:

你可能采取这样的思路：一个设计良好的框架，或一个深思熟虑、巧妙实现的架构，自然会在你的组织内被复用。事实是，即使最漂亮、最优雅、最可复用的架构、框架或系统，也只会被这样的人复用：

Know It’s There

知道它在那里

Within your organization, developers or designers need to know that a design, framework, library, or fragment of code exists, and where they can find all the critical information about these elements (e.g., documentation, versions, and compatibility) in order to reuse them. It is a simple, logical truth that people won’t look for things that they don’t believe exist. You are more likely to succeed with reusable elements if the information about them is “pushed.”

在你的组织内，开发或设计需要知道某个设计、框架、库或代码片段存在，以及在哪里能找到关于这些元素的所有关键信息（比如文档、版本、兼容性），才能复用。一个简单而逻辑的事实是：人们不会去找他们不相信存在的东西。如果关于可复用元素的信息被「推」出去，你成功的概率更高。

There are any number of methods for pushing information about reusable elements in an organization. These range from wiki pages with an RSS feed providing update information, useful in very large teams, to email announcing version updates in the source repository. In a tiny team, the designer or lead developer can inform his colleagues in personal conversations or by shouting it across the office. Ultimately, whatever your process for communicating about reusable elements, make sure you have one—don’t leave it up to chance.

组织里有很多推送可复用元素信息的方法。从带 RSS 提供更新信息的 wiki 页（在非常大的团队里有用），到邮件通知源码仓库的版本更新。在小团队里，设计师或首席开发可以在私下聊天里告诉同事，或者隔着办公室喊一嗓子。最终，不管你用什么流程沟通可复用元素，确保你有一个——别靠运气。

Know How to Use It

知道怎么用它

Understanding how to reuse an element depends on skills and training. Of course there are those people who (to use Donald Knuth’s terminology) “resonate” with coding and design. We have all worked with them, the gifted developers and architects whose speed and depth of understanding is impressive,

理解怎么复用一个元素取决于技能和培训。当然，总有那些人（用 Donald Knuth 的术语）对编码和设计「有共鸣」。我们都和他们共事过——那些天赋异禀的开发和架构师，理解速度和深度令人印象深刻，

even scary. But these people are rare. The rest of your team might be made up of good, solid, intelligent developers and designers. They need to be taught.

甚至吓人。但这些人很少。你团队里其他人可能是好的、扎实的、聪明的开发和设计。他们需要被教。

Developers and designers might not know of the particular design pattern used in a design, or fully understand the inheritance model that the framework designer intended them to use. They need to be given easy access to that information in the form of up-to-date documentation, or even better, training. A little training goes a long way toward ensuring that everyone is on the same page when it comes to reuse.

开发和设计可能不知道某个设计里用的特定设计模式，或不完全理解框架设计者期望他们用的继承模型。他们需要能方便地获得这些信息——以最新文档的形式，或者更好是培训。一点培训对确保大家在复用这件事上达成共识大有帮助。

Are Convinced That It’s Better Than Doing It Themselves

确信它比自己做更好

People, and particularly developers, tend to prefer to solve problems themselves rather than ask for help. Asking how something works is a sign of weakness, or even an indication of ignorance. This has a lot to do with the maturity and personality type of your individual team members; “better than doing it themselves” means different things to different people. The “young guns” on your team will always want to write things themselves because it appeases their egos, whereas your more experienced people are more likely to accept that someone else has given thought to the problem domain and has something to offer in terms of a solution.

人们，尤其是开发，倾向于自己解决问题而不是求助。问某个东西怎么用是软弱的表现，甚至是无知的标志。这和你团队成员各自的成熟度和人格类型关系很大；「比自己做好」对不同人意味着不同事。你团队里的「年轻枪手」总想自己写东西，因为这满足他们的自我；而你更有经验的人更可能接受别人已经思考过这个问题域、在方案上有可贡献的东西。

If your team doesn’t know where to find reusable artifacts or how to reuse them, they will default to the natural, human position: they will build it themselves. And you will pay for it.

如果你的团队不知道在哪里找可复用制品、或怎么复用它们，他们会默认回到自然的人的立场：自己造。而你会为此付出代价。

Jeremy Meyer Jeremy Meyer has been designing and developing software for nearly 20 years, as well as teaching its mastery. He is currently a principal consultant for Borland Software in its modeling and design space.

Jeremy Meyer Jeremy Meyer 设计和开发软件近 20 年，同时教授这门手艺。他目前是 Borland Software 建模和设计领域的首席顾问。

27. There Is No 'I' in Architecture

作者：Dave Quick

I know, there really is an ‘i’ in architecture. But it’s not a capital ‘I ’ , calling attention to itself, dominating discussion. The lowercase character fits neatly within the word. It’s there only because it fulfills requirements for proper spelling and pronunciation.

我知道，architecture 这个词里确实有个 i。但它不是那个大写的 I——不引人注目、不主导讨论。这个小写字母安安分分地待在词里。它在那里只是因为满足正确拼写和发音的要求。

How does that relate to us as software architects? Our egos can be our own worst enemy. Who hasn’t experienced architects who:

这和我们软件架构师有什么关系？我们的自我可能是自己最大的敌人。谁没见过这样的架构师：

think they understand the requirements better than the customers, •

觉得自己比客户更懂需求，

view developers as resources hired to implement their ideas, or •

把开发看作被雇来实现自己想法的资源，或者

get defensive when their ideas are challenged or ignore the ideas of others? •

自己的想法被挑战时就防御性起来，或者忽略别人的想法？

I suspect any experienced architect has fallen into at least one of these traps at some point. I’ve fallen into all of them and learned painful lessons from my mistakes.

我猜任何有经验的架构师都在某个时候掉进过至少一个陷阱。我全都掉进去过，从错误中学到了惨痛教训。

Why does this happen?

为什么会这样？

We’ve had success. • Success and experience build self-confidence and allow us to become architects. Success leads to bigger projects. There is a fine line between self-confidence and arrogance. At some point the project is bigger than our personal ability. Arrogance sneaks in when we cross that line but don’t know it yet.

我们成功过。成功和经验建立自信，让我们成为架构师。成功带来更大的项目。自信和傲慢之间只有一线之隔。某个时候项目大过我们个人能力。当我们跨过那条线却还不知道时，傲慢就溜进来了。

People respect us • . Tough design questions provide a critical safety net. Our own defensiveness, arrogance, or emphasis on our experience can result in missed design questions.

人们尊重我们。艰难的设计问题提供了一张关键的安全网。我们自己的防御性、傲慢、或对经验的强调，可能导致漏掉设计问题。

We’re human • . Architects pour themselves into each design. Criticism of your creation feels like criticism of you. Defensiveness is easy. Learning to stop it is hard. Pride in our accomplishments is easy. Recognizing our limitations without conscious effort is hard.

我们是人。架构师把自己倾注到每个设计里。对你作品的批评感觉像对你的批评。防御很容易。学会停止它很难。为成就骄傲很容易。不假思索就认识到自己的局限很难。

How do we avoid it?

怎么避免？

Requirements don’t lie • . With correct, complete requirements, any architecture that meets them is a good one. Work closely with the customer to make sure you both understand the business value each requirement provides. You don’t drive the architecture, the requirements do. You do your best to serve their needs.

需求不会说谎。有了正确、完整的需求，任何满足它们的架构都是好架构。和客户紧密合作，确保你们都理解每个需求带来的业务价值。不是你在驾驶架构，是需求在驾驶。你尽力服务它们的需要。

Focus on the team • . These are not just resources; they are your design collaborators and your safety net. People who feel unappreciated usually make a poor safety net. It’s the teams’ architecture, not yours alone. You provide guidance but everyone does the heavy lifting together. You need their help as much or more than they need yours.

关注团队。他们不只是资源；他们是你的设计协作者和安全网。觉得不被赏识的人通常做不出好安全网。这是团队的架构，不只是你的。你提供指导，但大家一起干重活。你需要他们的帮助，和他们需要你的一样多、甚至更多。

Check your work • . The model is not the architecture. It is only your understanding of how the architecture should work. Work with your team to identify tests that demonstrate how the project’s architecture supports each requirement.

检查你的工作。模型不是架构。它只是你对架构应该如何工作的理解。和团队一起识别那些能展示项目架构如何支持每个需求的测试。

Watch yourself • . Most of us fight our natural tendencies to defend our work, focus on our selfish interests, and see ourselves as the smartest person in the room. Pressure pushes these tendencies to the surface. Consider your interactions for a few minutes every day. Did you give everyone’s ideas the respect and acknowledgment they deserved? Did you react negatively to well-meaning input? Do you really understand why someone disagreed with your approach?

警惕自己。我们大多数人都在和自己的天性作斗争——为自己的工作辩护、关注私利、把自己看作房间里最聪明的人。压力会把这些天性推到表面。每天花几分钟想想你的互动。你给了每个人的想法应有的尊重和认可吗？你对善意的输入有过负面反应吗？你真的理解为什么有人不同意你的方法吗？

Removing the ‘I’ from architecture doesn’t guarantee success. It just removes a common source of failure that’s entirely your fault.

从架构里去掉「我」并不能保证成功。它只是去掉了一个完全是你自己过错的常见失败源。

28. Get the 1,000-Foot View

作者：Erik Doernenburg

As architects, we want to know how good the software is that we are developing. Its quality has an obvious external aspect—the software should be of value to its users—but there is also a more elusive internal aspect to quality, having to do with the clarity of the design, the ease with which we can understand, maintain, and extend the software. When pressed for a definition, this is where we usually end up saying “I know it when I see it.” But how can we see quality?

作为架构师，我们想知道自己在开发的软件有多好。它的质量有明显的外部方面——软件应该对用户有价值——但也有一个更难捉摸的内部方面，和设计的清晰度、我们理解、维护和扩展软件的难易程度有关。被追问定义时，我们通常最后会说「我看到了就知道」。但我们怎么看到质量？

In an architecture diagram, little boxes represent entire systems and lines between them can mean anything: a dependency, the flow of data, or a shared resource such as a bus. These diagrams are a 30,000-foot view, like a landscape seen from a plane. Typically the only other view available is the source code, which is comparable to a ground-level view. Both views fail to convey much information about the quality of the software: one is too high level and the other provides so much information that we cannot see structure. Clearly, what is missing is a view in between—a 1,000-foot view.

在架构图里，小方框代表整个系统，它们之间的线可以意味着任何东西：依赖、数据流、或像总线这样的共享资源。这些图是 3 万英尺视角，像从飞机上看风景。典型情况下唯一可用的另一个视角是源代码，相当于地面视角。两个视角都没能传达多少软件质量信息：一个太高，另一个信息太多以至于我们看不到结构。显然，缺的是中间的视角——1000 英尺视角。

This 1,000-foot view would provide information at the right level. It aggregates large amounts of data and multiple metrics, such as method count, class fan out, or cyclomatic complexity. The actual view very much depends on a specific aspect of quality. It can be a visual representation of a dependency graph, a bar chart that shows metrics at a class level, or a sophisticated polymetric view that correlates multiple input values.

这个 1000 英尺视角会在合适的层次提供信息。它聚合大量数据和多个指标，比如方法数、类扇出、或圈复杂度。实际视角很大程度取决于质量的哪个具体方面。它可以是依赖图的可视化、显示类级指标的柱状图、或关联多个输入值的复杂多变量视图。

Manually creating such views and keeping them in sync with the software is a hopeless endeavor. We need tools that create these views from the only true source, the source code. For some views—a design structure matrix, for example—commercial tools exist, but it is also surprisingly easy to create specialized views by combining small tools that extract data and metrics with generic visualization packages. A simple example would be to load the output from checkstyle, which is essentially a set of metrics on the class and method level, into a spreadsheet to render charts. The same metrics could also be shown as a tree-map using the InfoViz toolkit. A great tool to render complex dependency graphs is GraphViz.

手动创建这种视图并让它们和软件保持同步，是无望的努力。我们需要从唯一真实来源——源代码——创建这些视图的工具。有些视图（比如设计结构矩阵）有商业工具，但把提取数据和指标的小工具与通用可视化包组合起来，创建专门视图也出奇地容易。一个简单例子：把 checkstyle 的输出（本质上是类和方法级的一组指标）加载到电子表格里画图。同样的指标也可以用 InfoViz 工具包显示成 treemap。渲染复杂依赖图的好工具是 GraphViz。

Once a suitable view is available, software quality becomes a little less subjective. It is possible to compare the software under development with a handful of similar systems. Comparing different revisions of the same system will give an indication of trends, while comparing views of different subsystems can highlight outliers. Even with just a single diagram, we can rely on our ability to spot patterns and perceive aesthetics. A well-balanced tree probably represents a successful class hierarchy; a harmonious set of boxes might show code that is organized into appropriately sized classes. Most of the time a very simple relationship holds: if it looks good, it probably is good.

一旦有了合适的视图，软件质量就变得不那么主观。可以把开发中的软件和几个类似系统比较。比较同一系统的不同版本能看出趋势，比较不同子系统的视图能突出异常值。即使只有一张图，我们也能依靠自己发现模式和感知美学的能力。一棵平衡良好的树大概代表成功的类层次；一组和谐的方框可能显示代码被组织成大小合适的类。大多数时候一个非常简单的关系成立：如果它看起来好，它大概就是好。

Erik Doernenburg Erik Doernenburg is a technology principal at ThoughtWorks, Inc., where he helps clients with the design and implementation of large-scale enterprise solutions.

Erik Doernenburg Erik Doernenburg 是 ThoughtWorks 的技术负责人，帮助客户设计和实现大规模企业解决方案。

29. Try Before Choosing

作者：Erik Doernenburg

Creating an application requires Making many decisions. Some might involve choosing a framework or library, while others revolve around the use of specific design patterns. In either case the responsibility for the decision generally lies with the architect on the team. A stereotypical architect might gather all the information that can be gathered, then mull over it for a while, and finally decree the solution from the ivory tower for it to be implemented by the developers. Not surprisingly, there is a better way.

创建应用需要做很多决定。有些涉及选择框架或库，另一些围绕特定设计模式的使用。两种情况下，决定的责任通常在团队里的架构师身上。一个典型的架构师可能收集所有能收集的信息，琢磨一阵，最后从象牙塔里颁布方案让开发实现。毫不奇怪，有更好的办法。

In their work on lean development, Mary and Tom Poppendieck describe a technique for making decisions. They argue that we should delay commitment until the last responsible moment; that is, the moment at which, if the team does not make a decision, it is made for them—when inaction results in an outcome that is not (easily) reversible. This is prudent because the later a decision is made, the more information is available on which to base the decision. However, in many cases more information is not the same as enough information, and we also know that the best decisions are made in hindsight. What does this mean for the good architect?

在精益开发的工作中，Mary 和 Tom Poppendieck 描述了一种做决定的技术。他们主张应该把承诺推迟到最后负责时刻：也就是如果团队不做决定，决定就替他们做了——当不行动导致一个（不轻易）可逆的结果的时刻。这是审慎的，因为决定越晚做，可用来做决定的信息越多。然而，很多时候更多信息不等于足够信息，而且我们也知道最好的决定是事后才看清的。这对好架构师意味着什么？

The architect should constantly be on the lookout for decisions that will have to be made soon. Provided the team has more than a handful of developers and practices collective code ownership, the architect can, when such a decision point approaches, ask several developers to come up with a solution to the problem and go with it for a while. As the last responsible moment approaches, the team meets to assess the benefits and drawbacks of the different solutions.

架构师应该持续留意那些很快必须做的决定。如果团队有超过寥寥几个开发、并且实践集体代码所有权，当这样的决策点临近时，架构师可以请几个开发各想一个方案并试用一阵。当最后负责时刻临近，团队开会评估不同方案的利弊。

Usually, now with the benefit of hindsight, the best solution to the problem is apparent to everybody. The architect does not have to make the decision, he or she merely orchestrates the decision-making process.

通常，现在有了事后之明，最好的方案对每个人都显而易见。架构师不需要做决定，他或她只是协调决策过程。

This approach works for small decisions as well as for large ones. It can allow a team to figure out whether or not to use the Hibernate templates provided by the Spring framework, but it can equally answer the question of which JavaScript framework to use. The duration for which the different approaches evolve is obviously very dependent on the complexity of the decision.

这个方法对小决定和大决定都有效。它可以让团队搞清楚是否用 Spring 框架提供的 Hibernate 模板，也同样能回答用哪个 JavaScript 框架的问题。不同方案演化的时长显然取决于决定的复杂度。

Trying two or even more approaches to the same problem requires more effort than making a decision upfront and then just implementing one. However, chances are that an upfront decision leads to a solution that is later recognized to be suboptimal, leaving the architect with a dilemma: either the team rolls back the current implementation or it lives with the consequences, both of which result in wasted effort. Even worse, it is entirely possible that nobody on the team recognizes that the approach chosen is not the best one, because none of the alternatives was explored. In this case, effort is wasted without any chance of addressing the waste. After all, trying multiple approaches might be the least expensive option.

对同一问题试两甚至更多方案，比一开始就做决定然后只实现一个要花更多精力。然而，一开始做的决定很可能后来被认为是次优的，让架构师陷入两难：要么团队回滚当前实现，要么忍受后果，两种都导致浪费的精力。更糟的是，团队里完全可能没人认识到选的方案不是最好的，因为其他方案都没探索过。这种情况下，精力被浪费却没有任何机会去处理这个浪费。毕竟，试多个方案可能是最便宜的选项。

30. Understand the Business Domain

作者：Mark Richards

Effective software architects understand not only technology but also the business domain of a problem space. Without business domain knowledge, it is difficult to understand the business problem, goals, and requirements, and therefore difficult to design an effective architecture to meet the requirements of the business.

高效的软件架构师不仅懂技术，还懂问题空间的业务领域。没有业务领域知识，就很难理解业务问题、目标和需求，因此很难设计出满足业务需求的有效架构。

It is the role of the software architect to understand the business problem, business goals, and business requirements and translate those requirements into a technical architecture solution capable of meeting them. Knowing the business domain helps an architect decide which patterns to apply, how to plan for future extensibility, and how to prepare for ongoing industry trends. For example, some business domains (e.g., insurance) lend themselves well to a service-oriented architecture approach where as other business domains (e.g., financial markets) lend themselves more toward a workflow-based architecture approach. Knowing the domain helps you decide which architecture pattern may work best to satisfy the specific needs of the organization.

软件架构师的角色是理解业务问题、业务目标和业务需求，并把这些需求翻译成能满足它们的技术架构方案。了解业务领域帮助架构师决定应用哪些模式、怎么规划未来扩展性、怎么为持续的行业趋势做准备。比如，有些业务领域（比如保险）很适合面向服务架构方法，而另一些业务领域（比如金融市场）更适合基于工作流的架构方法。了解领域帮你决定哪个架构模式最能满足组织的特定需求。

Knowing the industry trends of a specific domain can also help a software architect in designing an effective architecture. For example, in the insurance domain, there is an increasing trend toward “on-demand” auto insurance, where you only pay for auto insurance when you actually drive your car. This type of insurance is great if you park your car at the airport on Monday morning, fly off to your work destination, and return Friday to drive back home.

了解特定领域的行业趋势也能帮软件架构师设计有效架构。比如，在保险领域，越来越多趋势是「按需」汽车保险——你只有在真的开车时才付车险。如果你周一早上把车停在机场、飞去工作目的地、周五再开回家，这种保险就很棒。

Understanding such industry trends enables you as a software architect to plan for these trends in the architecture, even if the company you are working with hasn’t planned for them yet as part of its business model.

理解这种行业趋势让你作为软件架构师在架构里为这些趋势做规划，即使你服务的公司还没在商业模式里规划它们。

Understanding the specific goals of the business also helps you design an effective architecture. For example, do the goals of the particular business you are working for include non-organic growth through heavy mergers and acquisitions? The answer to this question may influence the type of architecture you design. If the answer is yes, the architecture might include many layers of abstraction to facilitate the merging of business components. If the goals of the business include increased market share through a heavy online presence, then high availability is most likely going to be a very important attribute. As a software architect, always understand the goals of the company you are working with, and validate that the architecture can support these goals.

理解业务的具体目标也帮你设计有效架构。比如，你服务的特定业务的目标是否包括通过大量并购实现非有机增长？这个问题的答案可能影响你设计的架构类型。如果答案是是，架构可能包括多层抽象以方便业务组件合并。如果业务目标包括通过大量在线存在增加市场份额，那高可用很可能是非常重要的属性。作为软件架构师，始终理解你服务的公司的目标，并验证架构能支持这些目标。

The most successful architects I know are those who have broad hands-on technical knowledge coupled with a strong knowledge of a particular domain. These software architects are able to communicate with C-level executives and business users using the domain language that these folks know and understand. This in turn creates a strong level of confidence that the software architect knows what he or she is doing. Knowing the business domain allows a software architect to better understand the problems, issues, goals, data, and processes, all of which are key factors when designing an effective enterprise architecture.

我认识的最成功的架构师，是那些有广博动手技术知识、加上对特定领域深厚知识的人。这些软件架构师能用 C 级高管和业务用户熟悉的领域语言和他们沟通。这反过来建立起强烈的信心——这个软件架构师知道自己在做什么。了解业务领域让软件架构师更好地理解问题、议题、目标、数据和流程，这些都是设计有效企业架构的关键因素。
